A History of the Arab Peoples-About Albert Hourani

About Albert Hourani

Born in Manchester of Lebanese parents, Albert Habib Hourani studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Magdalen College, Oxford, where he was awarded a congratulatory first. From 1937 he taught for two years at the American University in Beirut; at the outbreak of war he joined the Royal Institute of International Affairs in London. In 1943 he went to Cairo to work as an analyst for the Foreign Office, and in 1946 he was among the experts giving evidence to the Anglo–American Committee of Inquiry on Palestine. With the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948 he returned to Oxford to take up a fellowship at Magdalen, and was soon appointed the first University Lecturer in the Modern History of the Near East. In 1958 he moved to St. Antony’s College, to become the first Director of the Middle East Centre, where, with the historian Elizabeth Monroe, he established a unique collection of papers on the Middle East. Under his guidance, Oxford emerged as one of the leading centres for the study of the Middle East in the English-speaking world. He held the Directorship until his retirement in 1979, but he was also visiting professor at a number of American Universities including Harvard, Chicago, Princeton and Philadelphia, as well as universities in Europe and the Arab World.

As teacher and author, he made a unique contribution towards 
understanding
 both the development of Arab nationalism and the complex relationship between Islam and the West. During his long and influential career he wrote eight books, edited seven others and published numerous articles. Upon the initial publication of 
A History of the Arab Peoples
, Edward Said wrote in the Independent that Hourani ‘is today’s leading historian of the Middle East, a scholar whose earlier books on 
Syria and Lebanon
, and on 
Arabic

Thought in the Liberal Age
 (an intellectual history of great insight and craftsmanship) are classics, mined both by scholars and general readers for their scope and their fastidious attention to the fabric of Arab life.’

Albert Hourani died in 1993.

A History of the Arab Peoples-About Malise Ruthven

About Malise Ruthven

Malise Ruthven is the author of Islam in the World, 
Islam: A Very Short Introduction, The Divine Supermarket: Shopping for God in America, A Fury for God: The Islamist Attack on America, Fundamentalism: The Search for Meaning
 and several other books. A former editor and scriptwriter with the BBC Arabic Service and World Service in London, he has taught Islamic studies and comparative religion at universities in Britain and the United States. His most recent book is 
Encounters with Islam: On Religion, Politics and Modernity.

A History of the Arab Peoples-Afterword 2012

Afterword 2012

In the two decades since Albert Hourani published his masterly overview of their history, the Arab peoples have experienced some momentous events, most recently the uprisings – known in the West as the ‘Arab Spring’ – that have challenged the existing order everywhere, and led to the fall of four long-established leaders in North Africa and Yemen while serving notice to all others. The protests and conflicts that dominated the international headlines throughout 2011 – with spectacular results in the fall of Zayn al-‘Abidin Ben ‘Ali in Tunisia, Husni Mubarak in Egypt, Mu‘ammar al-Qadhafi in Libya, and Ali Abdullah Saleh in Yemen – brought new dimensions of Arab political culture to the fore as protestors filled public spaces in their thousands and cities throughout the region echoed with demands for change. The long-term outcomes – at this writing – remained uncertain. Only Tunisia, where the movement began in late 2010, seemed destined to fulfil the universal aspiration for change by marking an orderly and constitutional transition to democratic governance under the Islamist Ennahda party. Elsewhere the transitions seemed more ambiguous, as the old order struggled to maintain its hold over state institutions, or groups that had been marginalized, or 
disenfranchised
, under the old system responded to the impulse for settling scores rather than the demand for open, public political space.

It would, of course, be absurd to suggest that the chain of events since the sad and unexpected death of Albert Hourani in 1993 could have been predicted by him. But none, I suspect, would have surprised him 
completely
. As a historian of ideas as well as events, his knowledge ran as deep as it was broad. He had a profound understanding of both the common legacies of religion and shared historical consciousness that hold the Arab peoples together, and of the ideological differences and structural forces that can tear them apart.

THE PERSISTENCE OF ‘
ASABIYYA

As suggested in the Preface (2012), Ibn Khaldun’s theories of dynastic and cyclical renewal and his concept of ‘
asabiyya
 – ‘a corporate spirit oriented towards obtaining and keeping power’ – still provide a serviceable prism through which recent events can be viewed. In its broader application the Khaldunian paradigm as interpreted by Hourani furnishes us with significant insights, despite the massive changes sustained by the 
Arab-Muslim
 world in the wake of European domination, beginning with the French conquest of Algeria in the 1830s and culminating in the defeat of the Ottoman Empire in 1918.

Writing in the late 1980s Hourani pointed out that in the post-colonial period, following an era of turbulence in the 1950s and early 1960s, there had been remarkably little change in the general nature of most Arab regimes or the direction of their policies. In Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, Jordan, Tunisia and Morocco there had been no dynastic changes for more than two generations; in Libya and Syria the regimes that had come to power around 1970 were still in place. In the Syrian Arab Republic, nearly a decade after Hourani’s book was published, leadership passed smoothly from father to son in 2000. At that time in Egypt and Libya dynastic successions were being widely discussed. As the UN Human Development Reports (referred to below) would suggest, the extent of that continuity was an indication of how durable the ‘
asabiyya
 of ruling elites – buttressed by modern methods of surveillance, brutality and bureaucracy – had remained under modern conditions.

The events of 2011 saw a cataclysmic change to this picture of apparent stability and continuity. Riots and demonstrations occurred in virtually every Arab country, with major insurgencies in Syria and Libya, civil uprisings in Tunisia, Egypt and Bahrayn, massive street demonstrations in Algeria, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Morocco and Oman and minor protests even in Saudi Arabia. Major causes of unrest included a dramatic rise in world food prices prompting industrial disputes, with sharpening 
perceptions
 of inequality and corruption on the part of swelling cohorts of educated but unemployed youth with access to social networks and sources of information outside governmental control. While there were common grievances, people’s aspirations varied in accordance with their countries’ distinctive political cultures, and the responses of government tended to differ according to a variety of factors, such as the depth of a country’s constitutional legitimacy, its sectarian or tribal affiliations and 
its capacity to ‘buy off’ opposition with social and economic handouts. A survey conducted by Cambridge University with a leading polling organization concluded that the ‘Arab Spring’ consisted of

a series of uprisings with different grievances, often different types of participants, and quite distinct types of political aspirations. But what appears to unite them is the very idea of the Arab Spring, within which supporters, activists and even opponents of political reform contextualize the protests they see in their own countries … The idea of the Arab Spring, the ideal of collective action spanning the region, is one that generates affiliations independently of the particularities of individual situations.

1

The political storm began, unexpectedly, in Tunisia, in the southern city of Sidi Bouzid, when a vegetable vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire in protest against his harassment by a municipal inspector. His action sparked a series of riots, as well as other self-immolations, that spread to the capital, Tunis, where riot police proved unable to control its momentum. When ordered by the President, Zayn al-‘Abidin Ben ‘Ali, to use the army to shoot the protestors, the chief of staff, General Rashid Ammar, refused.

2

 Ben ‘Ali flew with his family to exile in Saudi Arabia before a single shot was fired. A new government of ‘national unity’ was formed under a former prime minister, Mohammed Ghannouchi. Within days the impact of the Tunisian events was felt in Egypt. On 25 January protestors occupied Cairo’s Tahrir Square in a ‘Day of Rage’ directed against the regime of Husni Mubarak. Similar demonstrations took place in Alexandria and Suez. Some banners called for ‘Bread, freedom and social justice’; others proclaimed: ‘The people demand the fall of the regime’, or simply ‘IRHAL’ (‘Leave!’). Initially the government’s response was similar to Tunisia’s. The security police and 
baltagiyya
 ( thugs or criminals trained and paid for by the Dakhliyya, the Interior Ministry) were unleashed on the mainly youthful protestors, causing numerous deaths. As the novelist Ahdaf Soueif who witnessed these events described them:

In neighbourhoods across the country, through the night of this Friday that will become known as the Day of Wrath, the regime killed hundreds of Egypt’s young. Police and security men drove cars and trucks into groups of protestors. Snipers shot young men and women from the rooftops of the Ramses Hilton, the American University, the Egyptian Museum and the Dakhliyya (buildings surrounding Tahrir Square). Troops fired on them with shotguns and automatics, the thug militias, the 
baltagis
, burned them with Molotov cocktails and battered them with stones, ceramics and marble. Soldiers broke down and cried and were comforted by the revolutionaries.

3

Army helicopters swooped over the square and at one point the assembled throngs of protestors, now numbering hundreds of thousands, were ‘buzzed’ by low-flying F-16 jets. The protestors remained defiant, and in the end the army held back. According to widely circulated rumour an internal consultation of middle-ranking officers concluded that they would refuse orders to fire. It was said that when given the order to shoot by Mubarak, the chief of staff, Field Marshal Tantawi replied, ‘I can’t do it, Mr President.’

4

 At the subsequent trial of Mubarak, however, the prosecution failed to produce evidence of any such presidential command. In the event, as in Tunisia, the president’s fate was sealed by the army’s refusal to slaughter its fellow citizens.

On 11 February 2011 President Mubarak resigned after a three-decade tenure of office. The Constitution was suspended, and the parliament, long discredited by claims of electoral fraud, was dissolved. Power was transferred to the SCAF (Supreme Council of the Armed Forces) a 
committee
 of 20 generals chaired by Tantawi while preparations were made for the election and new parliament with a remit for drafting a new 
constitution
. But as Soueif herself comments, ‘a revolution is a process, not an event’.

5

 At the time of writing Egypt’s path from rebellion to functioning democracy is far from clear, with the military represented by SCAF still clinging to power in the face of the electoral success of the Muslim Brothers Freedom and Justice party. In the November 2011 parliamentary election the party won approximately 47 per cent of the vote and secured the election of its presidential candidate, Muhammad Morsi, the 
following
 June by a small majority over General Ahmad Shafiq, the last of Mubarak’s prime ministers. In an apparent attempt to pre-empt the outcome of the presidential election, the SCAF summarily dissolved the parliament on the basis of a constitutional court order citing technical violations of the electoral process, and issued a decree granting itself the continuing power to legislate, excluding any oversight by a future president. After being declared the winner, Morsi immediately reinstated the parliament in a direct challenge to the SCAF and the constitutional court’s Mubarak-appointed judges. As this edition went to press the stage was set for a struggle between the Islamist-dominated parliament and the constitutional court, with its military backers. Nevertheless despite some eight hundred civilian deaths in confrontations between protestors and the security forces, aided by 
baltagiyya
 thugs manipulated by remnants of the old regime, Egypt’s revolution, like Tunisia’s, has been a relatively orderly process. The contrast with neighbouring Libya and with Syria could not 
have been more stark. In both these countries the forces unleashed by the ‘Arab Spring’ would lead to civil war.

Even when governments, as in Egypt, tried to repress dissent by closing down the Internet, the images of rebellion, and notably the public humiliation of Mubarak, as he was booed and insulted when addressing protestors on giant public screens, were universally accessible through the satellite TV channels and mobile-phone networks that no regime had succeeded in repressing more than temporarily. As the Cambridge survey put it, ‘If people identify their national protest movements with the broader region-wide phenomenon of the ‘Arab Spring’, the perceived success of a civic uprising in one country will reinforce the estimations of the likelihood of similar achievements at home.’

6

 The fall of Mubarak, following closely on that of Ben ‘Ali, effectively broke a long-held taboo, exposing the essential fragility of all the regimes’ hold on power.

Within a week of Mubarak’s very public resignation rebellion had broken out in Libya. Its epicentre was Benghazi, Libya’s second city, and capital of the Cyrenaica region, which had been downgraded when Qadhafi concentrated power in the western capital of Tripoli more than a thousand kilometres away. With their city’s infrastructure neglected, despite the country’s wealth, the people of Benghazi had felt somewhat marginalized. Under Qadhafi’s Jamahiriyya or ‘State of the Masses’ the country was supposed to be governed through a series of People’s 
Congresses
 and Revolutionary Committees. Real power, however, including control of the all-important hydrocarbon sector, was concentrated in the somewhat eccentric hands of Qadhafi and his kinship network. Qadhafi stood apart from the formal institutions of state, styling himself ‘Brother Leader’ or Murshid (guide) in a highly visible, flamboyant style that combined elements of the Sufi 
shaykh
, the revolutionary activist and Western rock star. Despite the regime’s populist rhetoric and some real achievements – the highest per capita income in Africa ($12,000), good standards of healthcare, high rates of education, rising levels of female employment and massive infrastructural projects, such as the piping of fossil waters from the south through a gigantic ‘Man Made River’ – the mass of people, outside the ‘
asabiyya
 of the ruling group, were excluded from power. As Hugh Roberts commented:

The State of the Masses was in reality little more than a game to occupy and contain ordinary Libyans while the grown-up business of politics was conducted behind the scenes, the affair of a mysterious and unaccountable elite.

7

Benghazi, where the rebellion began, had retained some positive memories of the post-war Sanusi-based monarchy that Qadhafi had overthrown in 1969. Within days the city was in rebel hands, under the old Sanusi flag, and anti-government forces had taken control of neighbouring Misrata using makeshift transport and light weapons raided from the city’s arsenals. As protests erupted through the country the government initially lost control of most of the cities except for Tripoli, Qadhafi’s home town of Sirte and the southern city of Sabha. By the middle of March, however, Qadhafi’s loyalists had regrouped, regaining control of most of these cities except for Benghazi and Misrata.

With these cities threatened by artillery and aerial attacks, the United Nations Security Council, with the unanimous support of the Arab League, authorized NATO to impose a no-fly zone in order to protect civilians. Britain, France and Qatar (whose small airforce took part in the operations) interpreted the UN resolution proactively, to the dismay of several African and Arab League nations that had initially supported this move. As the war progressed, NATO air power became a strategic asset for the loosely co-ordinated, undisciplined and lightly armed opposition forces, compensating for their lack of armour and heavy artillery. Despite their denials, Britain and France, with backing from the United States, became active participants in a conflict aimed not just at the protection of civilians, but at changing a regime whose unpredictable, volatile leader had a long history of challenging Western interests in Africa and the Middle East. Qadhafi had actively opposed French interests in Africa, and Britain’s in Northern Ireland by providing weapons for the Provisional IRA – not to mention his claimed, if contested, responsibility for the bombing of a Pan-American airliner over the town of Lockerbie in Scotland in which 270 people were killed.

8

 Although Qadhafi had endeavoured to shake off his pariah status by renouncing plans to acquire nuclear arms and other weapons of mass destruction, he lacked the support of powerful friends in Europe and Asia. By late August opposition forces had taken Tripoli without encountering serious resistance. In September Mahmoud Jibril, the interim prime minister appointed by the opposition National Transitional Council (NTC), appeared before cheering crowds in Tripoli, while the French President Nicolas Sarkozy and British Prime Minister David Cameron landed in Benghazi to receive heroes’ welcomes, in recognition of their role in effecting ‘regime change’. The United Nations accorded recognition to the interim government’s envoys as Libya’s official representatives. Crude oil began flowing after an 
interval of several months, while Libya’s considerable financial holdings were transferred to the interim government.

In October 2011 Qadhafi was captured and killed by NTC fighters in Sirte. In a macabre inversion of the ritual lying-in-state accorded to national leaders, his blood-stained body was placed in a refrigerated meat cabinet, to be viewed by onlookers and, globally, through worldwide television coverage. With several of his sons killed in the fighting, his heir apparent Saif al-Islam held in the rebel city Zintan, and with other members of his clan in exile, the end of his regime was a certainty. But as in Egypt, the departure of the leader was no guarantee of stability. A general election in June 2012 produced an unexpectedly large turnout, placing the National Forces Alliance led by Mahmoud Jibril ahead of the Islamist parties linked to the Muslim Brothers. But security problems remained, with militias from cities such as Misrata and Zintan reluctant to succumb to central government control. Beyond Libya’s southern borders highly trained, well-armed mercenaries from the sub-Sahara Tuareg tribes that Qadhafi had used, Janissary-style, as his praetorians, were wreaking havoc in the Sahel states of Mali and Niger, where Qadhafi had invested heavily in pursuit of his African ventures. In Mali the failure of the government of Amadou Toumani Touré to deal with the Tuareg rebellion was cited as the reason for a military 
coup d’état
 mounted by junior army officers in March 2012.

THE CRISIS IN SYRIA

For the Middle East, the ramifications of Libyan conflict would be felt most acutely in Syria. Here the gruesome fate of the ‘Brother Leader’ and his coterie sent a strong message to the Asad regime which, unlike its Libyan counterpart, enjoyed the protection of powerful international supporters in Iran, Russia and China. Public protests in sympathy with the uprisings in Tunisia, Libya and Egypt, with increasingly vociferous demands for the regime’s overthrow, occurred throughout 2011, as thousand of protestors filled the streets and public spaces in al-Hasakah, Deraa, Deir ez Zor, Homs and Hama as well as the poorer suburbs of Damascus. Unlike in Egypt and Tunisia, however, elite army units remained loyal to the regime for many months. The escalating 
destructiveness
 and brutality of the repression, with loyalist Sabiha militias committing murderous onslaughts in the wake of tank and artillery attacks on rebel-held areas, produced an international and humanitarian 
crisis of growing proportions, with Syria’s ally Iran, backed by Russia and China, ranged against America and the West.

To begin with, the protests were mainly peaceful, with demonstrations gathering momentum at the funerals of victims (a toll of more than 20,000 at this writing). In due course the regime’s claim that it was facing an armed insurgency supported by unnamed foreign powers became 
self-fulfilling
, as defecting soldiers formed the opposition Free Syrian Army (FSA) that was sheltered, if not actively supported, by Turkey, with the likelihood that arms were being brought in from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and other Gulf states. As killing, maiming and torture took their toll, with major cities such as Homs and Hama subjected to escalating levels of bombardment, the FSA, though lightly armed, had offered temporary 
protection
 to citizens threatened with massacre, creating ‘liberated zones’ in places such as the Bab al Amr district of Homs and other areas where the regime’s writ had temporarily ceased to run. Early in 2012 an artillery assault on Homs, in which more than 200 people may have been killed prompted a resolution by the UN Security Council endorsing an Arab League peace plan requiring President Bashar al-Asad to hand power to his vice-president and enter into negotiations with the opposition. The resolution was vetoed by Russia and China on the ground that it violated Syria’s sovereignty and would open the way to outside military intervention, as in Libya.

The support of these major powers – both permanent members of the UN Security Council – was widely seen as giving the Syrian regime the ‘green light’ for renewed assaults on Homs and other rebel-held areas, not least because it was clear that as Syria’s leading arms supplier with a naval base in the port of Tartous Russia would oppose Western-backed demands by the Arab League for military intervention on the side of the rebels. In an ominous development a car bomb that killed 27 security personnel in Aleppo at the end of February 2012 was thought to have been the work of al-Qa‘ida in Mesopotamia, the militant Islamist organization or ‘franchise’ based in Iraq. As the conflict began spilling across Syria’s border with Lebanon, its dynamic threatened to engulf the whole region in a major upheaval. With the levers of power in the army and security apparatus held by members of the minority ‘Alawi sect to which Asad and his coterie belonged, the conflict acquired ominous sectarian overtones. The fragmented opposition accused the regime of rousing fears among Christians, Druzes, Isma‘ilis and other minorities (including some of the wealthier Sunni families who had benefited from the regime) that they 
would be vulnerable in the event of an outright opposition victory. In reality it appeared that it was the army that was responsible for most of the killings, although atrocities by opposition forces could not be ruled out.

In the context of what was rapidly becoming a nationwide civil war, the holding of a referendum in February 2012 leading to a new constitution in which the ruling Ba‘th party would cease to be the country’s sole political organization seemed nugatory, even frivolous, demonstrating a failure on the part of the regime and its external sponsors to appreciate the extent to which events on the ground had spiralled out of control. The regime’s violence, and the loyalties it commanded despite the scale of the opposition, were not primarily ideological. They were far from being the result of an emotional or philosophical commitment to a party that had long abandoned its agenda of promoting secular Arab republican values and aspirations. The regime’s durability lay rather in the complex web of tribal loyalties and networks of patronage and privilege underpinned by the ‘
asabiyya
 of the ‘Alawi religious bond.

9

The Syrian ‘Alawis, or Nusayris, who comprised less than 12 per cent of the population, had retained their grip on power since Hafez al-Asad, the ‘Alawi airforce commander, staged a successful coup against his Ba‘thist colleagues in 1970. Thereafter the power of the state – including the 
all-powerful

mukhabarat
 or intelligence apparatus – was concentrated in ‘Alawi hands. Of the officers commanding the 47th Syrian Tank Brigade responsible for suppressing the Muslim Brothers rebellion in the city of Hama in 1982 at a cost of some 20,000 lives, 70 per cent are said to have been ‘Alawis. When Hafez al-Asad died in June 2000 the constitutional niceties were rapidly dispensed with to ensure the succession of his son Bashar. Fearful that Hafez’s exiled younger brother Rifaat al-Asad would try to take over, a hastily convened session of the People’s Assembly voted to lower the minimum age for a president from 40 to 34, the exact age of Bashar al-Asad.

On his accession the younger Asad had tried to break free from his father’s Old Guard by sacking two of its leading figures, Vice-President Abd al-Halim Khaddam and the army chief of staff, Hikmat Shihabi. By and large, however, his efforts to reform the system that brought him to power were vacillating and inadequate. In the last resort he proved unwilling, or unable, to break the stranglehold of vested interests that had accrued around his predecessor. As David Gardner points out, the removal of two heavyweight figures who had provided ‘Sunni Muslim ballast for 
the minority Alawite rule camouflaged by the Ba‘th party’ merely served to ‘consolidate power for a family circle interested more in enrichment than in statecraft’.

10

 Bashar’s brother Maher, their brother-in-law Asif Shawkat and their cousin Rami Makhlouf had made personal fortunes out of trading in Lebanon, where Syria’s army and its ally Hezbollah held sway in the wake of Israel’s withdrawal to the south (where it continued to occupy a strip of territory) following its 1982 invasion. They also sold weapons, in violation of international sanctions, to Hafez al-Asad’s old rival, Saddam Husayn, in Iraq. Additionally Makhlouf had secured a lucrative monopoly in the licensed import of mobile phones.

Bashar al-Asad proved just as unwilling or unable to control the murderous proclivities of his father’s henchmen in Lebanon. In February 2005 the former prime minister Rafiq al-Hariri was killed along with 22 other people in a massive bomb attack on his motorcade in downtown Beirut. In line with Lebanon’s 1940 national pact (according to which the president is always a Christian, the prime minister a Sunni and speaker of the parliament a Shi‘i) Hariri, a Sunni, was a construction magnate who had succeeded in rebuilding Lebanon’s economy and much of its damaged infrastructure after the years of civil war culminating in the 1982 Israeli invasion. While this had benefited some Syrian business interests, Hariri’s success in building relationships between Lebanon’s divided communities fostered a nationalistic ‘Lebanon first’ mood – sometimes known as the ‘Cedar Revolution’ – that saw massive popular demonstrations against the presence of Syrian troops, prompting their withdrawal from Lebanon at the end of April 2005. The previous December, supported by Hariri, the UN Security Council had passed a resolution calling for the complete withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon and the disarming of its remaining militias, including Hezbollah. The resolution was a direct challenge to Syria’s presence in Lebanon. In March 2005 Syria’s ally, the Shi‘i-based militia Hezbollah, brought hundreds of thousands of Shi‘is onto the streets – a show of strength that was matched by 
counter-demonstrations
 from supporters of the Cedar Revolution. As ever Lebanese politics reflected the region’s wider geopolitical rivalries, with pro-Western forces backed by Saudi Arabia, where the Hariris had made their fortunes, pitched against the axis formed by Iran, Syria and Hezbollah. The following May, after a strong showing in the elections, Hezbollah joined the Lebanese government, becoming its most powerful bloc. In January 2011, after unseating the government led by Rafiq Hariri’s son Saad al-Din al-Hariri over its support for the UN investigations into 
the Hariri murder, Hezbollah acquired an effective veto over the 
government
 of Najib Mikati which came to power in June 2011.

After talks about integrating the Hezbollah militia into the regular armed forces broke down, Hezbollah attacked towns in northern Israel using missiles supplied by Iran, provoking an Israeli response that resulted in more than 1,500 civilian deaths. Israel’s failure to disarm the militia in the course of a 34-day war was converted into a propaganda victory that enabled Hezbollah – and their Iranian and Syrian backers – to present themselves as champions of those Palestinians who rejected the peace process intended to deliver a ‘two-state solution’ with Israel.

While Hezbollah remained a powerful political presence with close ties to Damascus, it was, arguably, the international investigation 
commissioned
 by the UN into the Hariri assassination that would have more far-reaching, long-term consequences. It led to the arrest of four Lebanese security chiefs, including General Mustafa Hamdan, head of the Presidential Guard and a close ally of the pro-Syrian president, Emile Lahoud. The UN report concluded:

There is probable cause to believe that the decision to assassinate the former prime minister Rafiq Hariri could not have been taken without the approval of 
top-ranked
 Syrian security officials and could not have been further organized without the collusion of their counterparts in the Lebanese security services.

11

As Gardner puts it, the UN investigation into the Hariri murder was a harbinger of the ‘Arab Spring’:

The spectacle of four generals in an Arab country’s security services being held over the assassination of a politician was not just unusual. It was unique. It 
electrified
 the Arab world, introducing into people’s minds the profoundly subversive idea that Arab despots, for long untouchable within a political culture of unbridled power and legal impunity, could be held to account.

12

TWO GULF WARS

From the 1980s to 2003 the trumping of ideology by the ‘
asabiyya
 of family interest was also apparent in Iraq, under the ruthless Ba‘thist regime of Saddam Husayn. In invading and occupying Kuwait in August 1990 (an event that occurred shortly after the first edition of this book went to press) Saddam Husayn had challenged not just Western interests, but the whole international system. His action was roundly condemned by the Arab League as well as the United Nations. All Iraqi and Kuwaiti assets 
were frozen, and the oil pipelines through Turkey and Saudi Arabia were cut. After an unprecedented build up of half a million US troops in Saudi Arabia, Iraqi forces were driven out of Kuwait in February 1991.

The American-led coalition in this first of two Gulf wars involving Western powers included Arab contingents from Saudi Arabia, Egypt and even traditionally anti-Western Syria, whose presence – along with that of other Muslim nations, such as Pakistan and Turkey – gave the campaign a legitimacy it would otherwise have lacked in Arab and Muslim eyes. Having restored Kuwaiti sovereignty, the US president, George H. W. Bush (a former head of the CIA and US Ambassador to the UN), forbore to pursue the Iraqi army into its own territory, fearing that this would weaken the coalition by embarrassing its Arab and Muslim allies. Despite the defeat of his army and the humiliating restrictions imposed on Iraq, with ‘no-fly’ zones policed by the US and British air forces and the establishment of an autonomous regional Kurdish government under de facto allied protection, Saddam Husayn’s regime survived. In response the regime exacted a brutal revenge on its internal enemies – especially Shi‘is in Iraq’s southern cities, who had expected coalition support for their brief rebellion against a government they had long since come to hate.

The survival of Saddam’s regime after its defeat in 1991 could partly be explained by the ‘
asabiyya
 of his al-Bu Nasr clan from the region of Tikrit, on the Tigris north of Baghdad, which radiated through an extended network of families, clans and tribes originating in this area. It was from this region in provinces dominated by Sunni Arabs (a 
demographic
 minority in Iraq, where at least 60 per cent of Arabic speakers are Shi‘is) that a significant part of the officer corps had been recruited prior to the military coup that brought Saddam Husayn and his former chief Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr to power in 1968. Though it formally adhered to the secular Arab nationalism of the Ba‘th party, the group’s ‘
asabiyya
 proved much more durable than its ideological orientation. By adroit manipulation of clan loyalties and rivalries, Saddam had built up a 
formidable
 system of power based not only on coercion and fear, but also on privilege and clientism.

The distribution of oil revenues and land, confiscated from old-regime landowners or political opponents, lay at the centre of this web of patron–client relationships. But a modern state such as Iraq had numerous other levers at its disposal in addition to oil and land: permits for setting up businesses, import–export enterprises (including armaments), control over 
foreign exchange and even labour relations. Behind the formal structures of the national state there existed what Charles Tripp usefully calls the ‘shadow state’ – the networks of associates, patrons and clients, along with ‘circles of exclusion and privilege emanating from the office and person of the president’. This ‘shadow state’, Tripp explains

was the real nexus of power. It stood behind all public state organizations, turning their hierarchies upside down and answering to a very different set of commands. At its heart were the men attached to the president through common regional background, family or tribal affiliation or tried-and-tested dedication to his 
personal
 service. Beyond them spread the networks of patronage and association that gave them weight in Iraqi society and established their worth to Saddam Husayn himself, whilst reinforcing their dependence on his favour.

13

Tripp estimates that this privileged element in Iraqi society consisted of approximately half a million people, including their dependants, out of a population of some 26 million. They were the people to whom Saddam Husayn harnessed his leadership, convincing them that he would further their interests and that they would lose everything if he fell from power.

14

The military arm of Saddam’s ‘
asabiyya
 was the Tikriti-dominated Republican Guard, preserved by him during Operation Desert Storm. It protected him during the risings by the Kurds in the north and the Shi‘a in the southern cities of Basra, ‘Amara, Nassiriyya, Najaf and Karbala in 1991. Though the Kurds were protected by allied air power, the Shi‘i insurgents were abandoned (despite initial encouragement by America). Within a few weeks the Republican Guard divisions had recaptured all the rebel-held towns, inflicting massive destruction and loss of life. Far from undermining the regime, the pariah status exemplified by the sanctions imposed on Iraq may have enhanced the Tikriti ‘
asabiyya
 that lay at its core. The ‘oil for food’ programme instituted by the United Nations under humanitarian pressure had the unintended consequence of strengthening the system of patronage and repression while enabling the regime to blame hostile powers, led by the United States, for the sufferings of the majority of its people.

The survival of the Ba‘thist regime remained ‘unfinished business’ that would haunt United States policy-makers for the next decade, especially the neo-conservatives who rose to positions of influence when George W. Bush (son of George H. W. Bush) became US president in January 2001. On 11 September that year the event that became known as ‘9/11’ provided the ‘hawks’ in Washington with their opportunity.

11 
SEPTEMBER
 2001

The attacks on New York and Washington on 11 September 2001 killed nearly 3,000 people in the most belligerent act to have occurred on the American mainland since the end of the Civil War. All nineteen of the suicide hijackers who flew civilian jets loaded with fuel and passengers into the World Trade Center in Manhattan and the Pentagon near Washington were Arabs. Fifteen of them were nationals of Saudi Arabia. All are believed to have received their training and funding from the al-Qa‘ida (‘base’ or ‘foundation’) network presided over by the Saudi dissident Osama bin Laden under the protection of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. Although no convincing evidence was produced linking bin Laden’s organization to the regime in Iraq, the ‘hawks’ in the US administration, led by Vice-President Dick Cheney and Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, insisted that the action in Afghanistan – where the Taliban regime was removed after a massive US aerial bombardment – must be followed by the overthrow of Saddam Husayn.

While any operational linkage between 9/11 and the Iraqi regime would remain unproven, a more complex narrative connected the attack on America to the Iraqi action in Kuwait. The son of a wealthy Yemeni contractor with close ties to the Saudi ruling family, bin Laden had built a reputation as a 
mujahid
 or ‘holy warrior’ in the struggle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan, a campaign – supported by many Muslim governments, as well as covertly by the CIA – that drew volunteers from many parts of the Arab world. When Iraq invaded Kuwait and seemed to threaten the Saudi oil fields, bin Laden offered his support to the king, suggesting a plan whereby he would train up Saudi militias using 
battle-hardened
 veterans from the Afghan 
jihad
. Fearing that his plan was ill thought out, as well as politically risky (since such a 
mujahidin
 army could pose a threat to the dynasty), the Saudi government rejected bin Laden’s proposal, taking instead the highly controversial step of entrusting the defence of the kingdom to American troops.

Bin Ladin’s opposition to the presence of ‘infidel’ troops in a country containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina was shared by many of Saudi Arabia’s most influential ‘
ulama
, including Shaykh Salman 
al-Awdah
, a leader of the Sahwa (‘Awakening’) group of clerics who were openly critical of Saudi Arabia’s ties to the West. For bin Laden and his followers (who included veterans of the Afghan struggle as well as 
militants
 from Egypt) the campaign to expel infidel forces from the ‘Land of the Two Holy Places’ – by attacking US targets everywhere – took 
precedence 

over the earlier project of overthrowing incumbent regimes to bring their societies closer to Islamic norms. Once the United States had been expelled from the area, bin Laden told his cohorts, its local clients would fall like ripened fruits.

15

THE AMERICAN OCCUPATION AND ITS AFTERMATH

In March 2003 the Iraqi regime collapsed in the face of an American invasion that was preceded by one of the severest aerial bombardments in the history of warfare. Saddam Husayn fled Baghdad, and remained in hiding until his discovery and arrest in December. The Iraqi army, including the elite Republican Guard, virtually melted away, with soldiers deserting en masse. The chosen American tactic of ‘shock and awe’ took a high toll of civilian life. Between 4,000 and 7,000 non-combatants are estimated to have been killed during the invasion in addition to between 7,000 and 12,000 members of the security forces.

16

 The relief and joy of many Iraqis at the fall of a hated regime was manifested in the spectacle – shown on television throughout the world – of people pulling down statues of Saddam Husayn and attacking other symbols of his rule. That moment did not last, however. A disastrous combination of factors plunged Iraq into an era as bleak as any suffered by its people in four decades of Ba‘thist rule: the destruction of the country’s infrastructure of roads, bridges, hospitals, power stations and water-treatment plants. Worse still was the absence of a coherent policy of post-war reconstruction.

The American administrator of the Coalition Provisional Authority, Ambassador Paul Bremer, took two decisions that would have dire 
consequences
. He disbanded all the existing Iraqi security forces and dissolved the Ba‘th party, banning its senior members from serving in the public sector, thereby excluding the country’s most able and experienced officials from the administration. Early results of the invasion were a collapse of civil governance, widespread criminality and the wholesale looting of property, including priceless archaeological treasures. In the longer term, disbanding the army, sending some 400,000 unemployed young men, trained in the use of weapons, back into their neighbourhoods accelerated the drift towards sectarian conflict and civil war. Behind the protective barriers of their headquarters in Baghdad’s Green Zone, the Americans appeared more interested in profiting from the invasion than establishing an effective post-war government. American companies received lucrative 
contracts, to the virtual exclusion of Iraqi firms, in a bonanza that allowed for ‘the inflation of budgets, the misappropriation of funds and the squandering of resources’.

17

 The nadir of Bremer’s regime was disclosure – which received massive international publicity – of the systematic 
humiliation
 and torture by American military personnel of Iraqi prisoners held at the notorious Abu Ghraib prison where Saddam’s enemies had once been murdered and tortured.

The invasion shattered the Iraqi state’s public institutions; but, as Tripp points out, the constituents of ‘shadow state’ – the networks of loyalty and ‘
asabiyya
 – were able to regenerate and reconstitute themselves in the rubble of the old state’s collapse. The invaders found that ‘the “shadow state” itself disintegrated into its myriad components and that these, far from evaporating, fell back on their local ties and communities, 
positioning
 themselves to re-form according to the new dispensations of power’.

18

 The lethal edges of these local networks of solidarity were the armed militias that engaged with each other as well as with the occupation forces. Within four months of the invasion the Americans, far from being seen as liberators, were facing insurgencies from both Sunni and Shi‘i forces. The 3,000-odd deaths the insurgents inflicted on the American occupation forces during the first three years, using a variety of tactics and weaponry such as suicide car bombs, rocket-propelled grenades and IEDs (
improvised
 explosive devices), turned the tide of US domestic opinion against the war, and contributed to the victory of the Democrats in the 2006 congressional elections and the election of Senator Barak Obama (who had voted against the war) as US president in November 2008. But the wounds suffered by America and its allies were minor compared with those inflicted on the Iraqis as a result of allied action, or those that they inflicted on each other, as inter-communal strife became increasingly violent. A report published in October 2004 – eighteen months after the invasion – put the overall figure of Iraqi deaths at 100,000. Although this was disputed by allied and Iraqi authorities who claimed a much lower figure of 30,000, at the end of 2006 the United Nations estimated that Iraqi civilians were being killed at a rate of 100 per day.

In June 2004 the Americans formally handed civil power to an interim government charged with the task of holding elections for the transitional national assembly that would draft a new constitution. The government, headed by Ayad ‘Allawi, a secular-minded Shi‘i, faced armed opposition from Sunni insurgents and former Saddam loyalists concentrated in the strategic town of Fallujah, west of Baghdad, as well as from the Mahdi 
army led by the populist Shi‘i cleric Muqtada al-Sadr. Al-Sadr’s base was in the poorest Shi‘i districts of Baghdad. But his power stretched into all the southern cities. His supporters confronted the Americans in the holy city of Najaf and – with other militias – eventually forced their British allies to withdraw from the streets of Basra. The American occupation of Fallujah, intended to crush the Sunni insurgency and clear Iraq of ‘foreign fighters’, was achieved at the cost of some 5,000 lives, many of them civilians. A pyrrhic victory at best, it prompted the withdrawal from the interim government of the leading Sunni party, reinforcing the impression that after centuries of dominance the Sunni Arab minority was now a target for vengeance. The general elections, held in January 2005, were boycotted by much of this constituency. The overall victors were two Shi‘i parties endorsed by Iraq’s senior Shi‘i cleric, the venerable Grand Ayatollah Sayyid Ali al-Husayni al-Sistani. Between them they won more than half the parliament’s seats with nearly 50 per cent of the vote. With Kurdish nationalists and Shi‘i Islamists commanding more than 
three-quarters
 of the seats the Sunni Arabs – some 20 per cent of the population – were virtually unrepresented. After interventions by al-Sistani and the US Embassy the balance was somewhat restored. Despite Sunni Arab calls for its rejection, a new constitution was approved by a plebiscite of 78 per cent to 22 per cent, with the Shi‘i and Kurdish provinces voting in favour, and the Sunni Arab provinces against.

Predictably the Shi‘i parties emerged victorious in the general elections for the new Iraqi democracy in December 2005, but without an overall majority. The voting conformed to patterns of ethnicity and religious affiliation, rather than ideology.

The following April Jalal Talabani, the veteran Kurdish leader, was sworn in as president, a largely symbolic role. A new government, under Nuri al-Maliki of the Shi‘i Da‘wa party, took office in May. In theory the American neo-conservatives’ project for spreading democracy ‘from above’, using military force if necessary, had come to fruition.

The reality was much more complex. The forms of the new Iraqi democracy were being established against a rising tide of violence and sectarian terror that threatened to pull the country apart. While ministers talked and jostled for position, the armed units proliferated on the ground. By December 2006 there were many more men under arms than there had been in the final years of Saddam’s regime. They served a bewildering variety of masters, often mutually antagonistic, in the state security forces reconstituted and trained by the Americans, or in the militias controlled by 
the parties in government. In an atmosphere of paranoid insecurity no one could be sure if a man in uniform was a ‘genuine’ soldier or policeman, a criminal, or member of a death squad.

The impression that the government was dominated by Shi‘i factions bent on revenge was reinforced in December 2006 by the execution of Saddam Husayn, after his conviction on charges of unlawful killing and crimes against humanity. His hanging took place on the day that Sunnis – but not the Shi‘a – celebrate the ‘Id al-Adha (Feast of Sacrifice), marking the end of the annual pilgrimage to Mecca. An unofficial video, widely broadcast, showed undignified scenes of men – apparently followers of Muqtada al-Sadr – taunting him while he in turn denounced them from the scaffold.

19

Sectarian atrocities multiplied, many of them blamed on the Iraqi branch of al-Qa‘ida – a group loosely affiliated to the bin Laden network and characterized by its extreme anti-Shi‘i views. After January 2007, however, the levels of violence began to subside. The US deployed five additional brigades (20,000 troops) in al-Anbar province. They began funding Sunni tribal groups, including former insurgents, known as the ‘Awakening Councils’, who had come to resent the presence of al-Qa‘ida and its foreign fighters. Concerned that these Sunni groups would 
complicate
 matters by developing into a ‘third’ military force, the Maliki government took steps to integrate them into the official Iraqi armed forces.

In 2008 the Iraqi parliament signed a security agreement with the United States requiring that all US forces be withdrawn from Iraq by the end of 2011. Military decisions governing US forces would be taken by a joint committee of American and Iraqi officers, with combat troops to be removed from Iraqi towns and villages by mid-2009. The agreement was welcomed by the incoming administration of US President Obama, who had campaigned to end the war in Iraq with a view to concentrating US military efforts in Afghanistan.

The parliamentary elections in March 2010 proved highly controversial, after some 456 candidates were banned for having alleged links with the Ba‘th party. With 91 deputies ‘Allawi’s secular-oriented coalition – the Iraqiyya or Iraqi National Movement – held the largest block of seats, two more than Maliki’s group. The elections were held under a new ‘open-list’ system – endorsed by Sistani – whereby voters were able to vote for individuals as well as party lists. After months of tortuous negotiations, however, Maliki retained the premiership, with Talabani retaining the 
presidency and ‘Allawi heading a new security council. Under a 
power-sharing
 formula encouraged by the United States, Tariq al-Hashimi, leader of the Iraqiyya, remained vice-president, despite his persistent demands for higher Sunni representation and an end to Maliki’s de-Ba‘thification policies. At the end of 2011, however, and within weeks of the departure of the last American troops, the government issued a warrant for Hashimi’s arrest on terrorist charges, causing the vice-president to take refuge in the semi-autonomous northern region under Kurdish control and, later, in Turkey. With Hashimi’s departure the seal was set for an unambiguously sectarian regime with little democratic credibility beyond the fact that its constituent Shi‘i parties represented a more substantial portion of Iraq’s population than the minority Sunnis who had formed the backbone of the former Ba‘thist regime.

THE SECTARIAN DIMENSION

While the ‘Arab Spring’ challenged the legitimacy of ruling dynasties and incumbent elites throughout the region, in confessionally mixed 
communities
 it raised the growing spectre of sectarian conflict, as long suppressed social forces were mobilized along with feelings of public insecurity. In 2004, anticipating the victory of the Shi‘i parties in the Iraqi parliamentary elections, King ‘Abdullah of Jordan – who inherited the throne on the death of his father, King Husayn, in 1999 – warned of a ‘Shi‘i Crescent’ stretching from Iran into Iraq, Syria and Lebanon, that would be dominated by Tehran. The idea was echoed by the Saudi foreign minister, who described the US intervention in Iraq as a ‘handover of Iraq to Iran’, while President Mubarak of Egypt claimed that Shi‘is residing in Arab countries were more loyal to Iran than to their own countries. With Saudis, Qataris and other Gulf rulers urging the arming of the Syrian opposition, if not direct military intervention, the wider configurations of power appeared to be settling along fault lines reflecting the centuries-old historic competition between the two non-Arab empires of Ottoman Turkey and Safavid-Qajar Iran, where imperial ambitions had been buttressed by the Sunni–Shi‘a religious divide.

20

 In Bahrayn democratic protests by the Shi‘a, who comprise around 70 per cent of the population, were brutally suppressed by the government with the aid of Saudi troops and Sunni mercenaries imported from Jordan, Pakistan and the United Arab Emirates. Under the Sunni al-Khalifa regime dating back to 1783, the Shi‘a of Bahrayn had suffered decades of discrimination. While their 
demands for greater political participation, access to employment and constitutional limitations on power were rarely expressed in sectarian terms, their leaders and supporters were overwhelmingly Shi‘a. The security forces – including personnel recruited from outside Bahrayn – were almost exclusively Sunni.

Throughout the Gulf region the revival of Arab Shi‘ism, attested by the Iraqi government, seemed likely to challenge the hegemony of Sunni Arab dynastic rule that prevailed in much of the region in the wake of the colonial departure. A democratic strand in Shi‘ism – at variance with the Khomeinist ideology prevailing in Iran – had intellectual roots in Iraq in the teachings of late Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr and the Ayatollah Sistani. Both regarded the voice of the people as a legitimate source of legislation and hence of the divine will:

Islamic theory rejects monarchy as well as the various forms of dictatorial 
government
; it also rejects aristocratic regimes and proposes a form of government which contains all the positive aspect of the democratic system.

21

Unlike Khomeini, Sistani precluded clerics from holding public office. He had urged Iraqis to vote in multi-party elections as a religious duty. His clarion call for democracy had a powerful impact on Arab Shi‘i 
communities
 far beyond Iraq’s borders. In 2005 some 50,000 protestors, spearheaded by the al-Haq movement, took to the streets in Manama in Bahrayn, where 70 per cent of the population is Shi‘i, demanding full legislative powers for parliament. The king responded by co-opting the more pliant Shi‘i party into parliament while forming closer ties with the Salafists and staffing the security services with Sunnis imported from tribal areas of Pakistan and Yemen and Sunni communities in Syria.

22

 Thereafter the Bahrayni government and their Saudi supporters routinely accused the Iranians of being behind the protests, using televised confessions of detainees to support claims that were strongly rejected by activists. In March 2011 the Saudis sent tanks across the causeway linking their territory to Bahrayn, in order to clear peaceful demonstrators from the traffic circle in Pearl Square, main venue for the protests. Despite the American government’s support for regime change in Libya and Syria, it remained firmly committed to the unequal and undemocratic status quo in Bahrayn. As host to the US Navy’s Sixth Fleet, the island kingdom acted as a vital Western shield for Saudi Arabia.

23

The Americans and their Saudi allies feared that sectarian conflict in Bahrayn could spread to the country’s oil-bearing Eastern Province where 
most of the kingdom’s Shi‘is, who number more than a million and a half, are concentrated. Under pressure from the Shi‘a and other reformers, as well as his American allies, the Saudi monarch made the minimal gesture of authorizing municipal elections containing a democratic component. Although there were numerous restrictions, with half the seats appointed, political parties banned and women barred from standing, Saudi Shi‘is followed Sistani’s lead by voting in large numbers, while Shi‘i intellectuals joined with prominent Salafists including Salman al-Awdah in demanding reforms leading to a constitutional monarchy, an elected parliament, respect for human rights and an end to anti-Shi‘i discrimination. While such demands went far beyond anything the regime was likely to concede, the ‘thresholds of arrest’ had been lifted slightly, enlarging the margins of political space allowed in the kingdom.

24

The dynasty’s other tactics included the familiar measures of patronage and co-option. In its initial response to local unrest inspired by the ‘Arab Spring’ in 2011 the Saudi goverment increased its spending on housing and other social benefits to the tune of US $130 billion, a move assisted by the rise in oil prices occasioned by economic sanctions imposed on Iran by the United States and the European Union. Both powers, along with Israel, were expressing increasing alarm at the Islamic Republic’s development of a nuclear-energy programme that could be converted to military use. There remained great uncertainty, however, about the Saudi regime’s 
long-term
 durability, not least because of the structural flaw in its system of royal succession. With the sons of ‘Abd al-‘Aziz Ibn Sa‘ud now reaching their ninth decade, the selection of the first of his grandsons as king would have to be managed with exceptional deftness if the dynastic autocracy was to survive into a third generation.

REBELLION IN YEMEN

The Sa‘udi dynasty’s anxieties were deepened by events in Yemen, where a revolt inspired by events in Egypt and Tunisia finally induced the 
resignation
 of President Ali Abdullah Saleh after many months of prevarication. In January 2012 Saleh, who had been wounded in an armed attack on his palace the previous year, finally relinquished power to his deputy after reluctantly agreeing to a formula brokered by the United States and Gulf Co-operation Council countries (including Saudi Arabia) exempting him, his family and supporters from prosecution for corruption and human rights violations. The main opposition groups endorsed the transfer of 
power, confirmed by the election of Saleh’s former deputy ‘Abd Rabuh Mansur al-Hadi, the only candidate, on a claimed turnout of more than 60 per cent. The new government, however, was rejected by rebels belonging to the Houthi movement based in the Zaydi branch of the Shi‘a who had been waging a long insurgency against the government from their base in the mountainous region around Sa‘da with alleged support from Iran. The conflict drew on anti-Saudi feeling from the early 1990s when the Riyadh government expelled nearly a million Yemeni workers to punish Saleh’s government for supporting Saddam Husayn’s occupation of Kuwait. A deeper strand of anti-government resentment, however, appeared to be a general feeling of exclusion, based on the perceived political, economic and religious marginalization of the Zaydis since the end of the imamate in 1962. Building on the government’s perceived neglect of the north, and influenced by the Zaydi doctrine of lawful resistance to unjust rule, the Houthi movement shared aspects of the Shi‘i revival elsewhere in the region. It was counterbalanced by an Islamist rebellion based in the 
formerly
 separate state of South Yemen fostered in part by business interests opposed to the government in San‘a.

THE PALESTINE CONFLICT

After 9/11 and the second Bush administration’s ‘war on terror’ the Palestinian rejectionists, led by the Islamist Hamas movement, gained support among Palestinians disillusioned by the corruption of the Palestine National Authority and its failure to realize the promise of a Palestinian state, as envisioned under the Oslo Accords. President George W. Bush’s insistence that the whole world, including the Arab-Muslim part of it, must join his ‘war against terror’ was interpreted by the Israeli government of Ariel Sharon as giving Israel the ‘green light’ to reoccupy Palestinian cities vacated under the Accords in order to flush out, kill or bring to justice the Palestinian factions responsible for suicide attacks against Israeli civilians. In an escalating ‘asymmetrical’ conflict, between Palestinians armed with home-made devices (including suicide vests) and the Israeli Defence Forces, Palestinian Arabs suffered disproportionately: in the period known as the second 
intifada
 which began in September 2000, 3,062 Palestinians were killed up to February 2005 compared with 970 Israelis. More than 20 per cent of the Palestinians killed were children under 18 compared with under 9 per cent of Israelis (most of them victims of suicide missions). In addition to blowing up the Arab homes to discourage 
families from harbouring terrorist suspects, the Israelis adopted a tactic of assassinating leaders held responsible for terrorist operations. The most prominent victims were Shaykh Ahmad Yassin, leader of Hamas, the Islamic Resistance Movement, in March 2004 and his successor, Dr ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Rantissi, the following month. More than 300 Palestinians were killed as a result of the ‘collateral damage’ inflicted in the course of this campaign. Although the West Bank suffered major disruption and a collapse of its economy, the Gaza strip – possibly the most densely populated region on the planet – suffered most, with more than 24,000 people rendered homeless by Israeli demolitions. The following year, in August 2005, the Israeli government withdrew unilaterally from Gaza, removing some 9,000 Jewish settlers and dismantling all its military bases.

As a measure to protect the Israeli population from suicide missions the government embarked on the construction of an 8-metre-high concrete barrier along the ‘green line’ separating Israel from the Occupied West Bank. While greatly reducing the number of bomb attacks, the barrier inflicted additional hardships on a population already demoralized by Israeli security measures including lengthy delays at security checkpoints. In places the barrier separated farmers from their lands, even children from their schools, while preventing Palestinians from travelling within the West Bank or seeking work in Israel. In a 14–1 ruling in July 2004 the International Court of Justice ruled that the barrier violated 
international
 law.

The succession of Mahmoud Abbas, the leader of al-Fatah, as President of the Palestinian Authority after Yasir ‘Arafat’s death in 2004 did little to relieve Palestinian frustrations. As the human rights activist and Palestinian legislator Hanan Ashrawi had explained in her submission to the United Nations team in 2002:

Prevented from laying claim to our resources and rights, we witness our lands being confiscated and our crops and trees destroyed. Israel military checkpoints fragment our human and territorial continuity and have become the most brutal expression of a discriminatory and pervasive system of wilful humiliation and subjugation. All rights – including the right to shelter, to educational and health services, to work; to a clean and untainted environment; to a life free from war, fear and coercion; to governance as an expression of the collective will for internal justice and to gain access to the tools of information and knowledge – have been obliterated.

No instruments have been devised to measure such wholesale destruction. A quantitative approach may be possible for the assessment of the number of 
hectares confiscated, trees uprooted, victims murdered or injured, jobs lost and income severed. However the human mind has not succeeded in measuring the full import of the loss of hope and the usurpation of the future of a whole nation. Nor can the collective and individual traumas of children in the grip of horror and fear be quantified – despite the frequency of nightmares, bedwetting incidents and uncontrollable behaviour.

25

The desperation and frustrations of Palestinians under occupation, 
combined
 with the perception of corruption in the Fatah-controlled Palestinian Authority, accounted for the victory that gave the Islamist Hamas 
movement
 a majority of seats in the Palestinian legislative elections in January 2006. Hamas is not party to Palestinian agreements recognizing Israel, and although its leaders have made statements allowing for an indefinite ‘truce’ with the Jewish state, its charter contains material derived from European anti-Semitism and calls for an end to the Jewish state. Numerous countries, including the United States, have designated it as a terrorist organization. After efforts to form a Palestinian unity government broke down, open fighting broke out between Hamas and security forces 
controlled
 by the PLO, with Hamas taking over in Gaza, leaving Mahmoud Abbas in control of the West Bank. In 2007, with tacit US support, Abbas mounted a quasi-constitutional coup in which he sacked Hamas premier Isma‘il Haniyya, appointing an unelected government under the capable and energetic Salam Fayyad, a former World Bank economist. While Fayyad succeeded in building up the Palestinian economy and improving the Authority’s institutions, hopes that his strategy would advance the cause of peace were frustrated by Israel’s persistence in building Jewish settlements on occupied Palestinian land, despite US disapproval and international condemnation.

The impasse in peace negotiations – largely caused by Israel’s refusal to freeze its settlement activities – prompted Abbas to increase international pressure on Israel by making a formal application for UN membership. Although the Obama administration made it clear that the US would veto the application in the Security Council (a prerequisite for full membership) Abbas’s initiative received widespread support from members of the General Assembly and produced an upgrading in Palestinian 
representation
 in UN bodies such as UNESCO.

The PLO–Hamas conflict reflected the wider geopolitical tensions afflicting the region. Although overwhelmingly Sunni (there are no Palestinian Shi‘i communities), Hamas drew its military, political and financial support from ‘the Shi‘i Crescent’ of Iran, Syria and Hezbollah, in 
addition to charitable funds from Saudi Arabia and the Gulf. After Mahmoud Abbas sacked the Hamas prime minister Isma‘il Haniyya in 2007, the United States and the European Union resumed financial aid to his administration, which governed under emergency decrees.

A counter-coup by Hamas in the Gaza strip produced a bizarre situation, with a population under siege, deprived of the most basic commodities, while smugglers earned fortunes by controlling the illegal importation of goods from Egypt through a network of underground tunnels. Operation Cast Lead, launched by Israel in December 2008 after the breakdown of a long ceasefire in which rockets were launched into Israel from Gaza, killed some 1,400 Palestinian civilians in an action seen by some of Israel’s supporters as ‘delegitimizing’ the Jewish state. Far from punishing or displacing Hamas, the pulverizing of Gaza by aerial bombardment with co-ordinated naval and ground attacks – along with a subsequent attack by Israeli commandos on a Turkish flotilla bearing activists with humanitarian supplies – served to consolidate Hamas’s grip on power. In 2011, weakened by the turmoil in Syria and the collapse of the Egyptian economy, the Hamas leadership succumbed to pressure from Qatar and other Gulf states to form a technocratic unity government under the leadership of Abbas. However, given the uncertainties raised by the ‘Arab Spring’, and with Israel stating it would refuse to have dealings with a government containing a ‘terrorist’ organization, there was no certainty that effective peace talks would be resumed.

A solution to the Palestinian conflict had long been mapped out as a possibility. In 2002, before Israeli tanks had moved into territories 
controlled
 by the Palestinian National Authority under the Oslo Accords, the Arab League, on the initiative of Saudi Arabia, had taken the 
historically
 important step of unanimously agreeing to recognize Israel and to normalize relations with it (including diplomatic exchanges, trade and tourism) in exchange for Israel’s withdrawal from territories it occupied in the 1967 war. Such a solution, however, though widely supported 
internationally
, failed to take account of the changes on the ground, and in particular the expanding Israeli settlements in and around Jerusalem.

DYNASTIC CONTINUITIES

Under modern conditions the traditional group loyalties of ‘
asabiyya
 – based on clan or personal allegiances – have been reinforced by 
bureaucratic
 methods, including police-state methods that would not have been 
available to governments in pre-colonial times. Such spheres of autonomy – in religious governance, the management of 
waqfs
 and educational foundations – as existed in the pre-colonial era had been eroded by government since late Ottoman times. In the words of the 2005 UN Arab Human Development Report,

the cycle through which the foundation of a law-based state and an independent civil society resistant to oppression might have been established was never 
completed
. Thus the [new] nation-state faced little difficulty in compromising the foundations of citizenship and civil relations, especially in the name of overcoming its economic dependency and catching up with developed countries.

26

As Hisham Sharabi, a leading Palestinian-American scholar, has suggested, ‘
asabiyya
 became the default position in most Arab societies: ‘Neither the city, nor the society, nor the state succeeded in developing formations capable of producing authentic alternative structures.’

27

While the persistence of forms of ‘
asabiyya
 appeared almost universal, there were obvious variations in the way that group solidarities applied themselves constitutionally. In Syria the ‘
asabiyya
 of the ‘Alawi clans exploited the spurious legitimacy of the one-party state based on an East European model (with some East European guidance) by infiltrating and taking over the Ba‘th party apparatus. Older forms of legitimacy conferred by conquest under Ottoman rule in the cases of Kuwait and other Gulf shaykhdoms, may prove more durable, despite the upheavals of the ‘Arab Spring’, suggesting avenues that opened in the direction of more organized systems of constitutional rule, if not full-blown Western-style democracies.

Despite the formal constitutional difference between Syria, a republic, and Jordan, a monarchy, the succession of Bashar al-Asad on the death of his father in June 2000 bore a striking resemblance to events that occurred in Amman sixteen months earlier. In February 1999 King Husayn, who was terminally ill with cancer, promoted his eldest son ‘Abdullah to Crown Prince. The move dismayed the supporters of his younger brother Prince Hasan, who had exercised the regency during the monarch’s absence for medical treatment in America. A letter the king is reported to have sent his brother expressed dissatisfaction with Hasan’s handling of the kingdom’s affairs during his absence, particularly his involvement in military matters. The dying monarch was also said to have accused his brother’s supporters of slandering his immediate family, prompting speculation about a serious rift within the Hashemite clan. In the event the Jordanian succession, like 
that of Syria, passed off smoothly. Prince Hasan was effectively excluded from power and several of his political allies were replaced.

Despite the continuing tensions stemming from second Palestinian 
intifada
 and the failure of the Oslo peace process, the continuity and legitimacy of the Hashemite monarchy did not appear to be at issue at this writing. King ‘Abdullah responded to the unprecedented volume of protest rallies and street demonstrations inspired by the events in Tunisia and Egypt by dismissing governments for being too slow in enacting anti-corruption measures, such as the prosecution of officials accused of insider dealings in the privatization of utilities such as water. While an unusual level of co-operation between the traditionally loyal East Bank tribes and the Islamic Action Front (an arm of the Muslim Brothers) put pressure on the monarchy, the events in neighbouring Syria had the effect of dampening the momentum of civil unrest, leaving the monarchy and its military backers in charge.

In Morocco, the ‘Alawite monarchy whose legitimacy, like that of the Hashemites, derives from the king’s descent from the Prophet Muhammad, also experienced a smooth dynastic transition. Muhammad VI, who succeeded his father Hasan II in July 1999, immediately 
proclaimed
 himself an advocate of reform and modernization, adopting a high-profile populist style very different from that of his father. Some ground for change had been prepared during the final years of his father, who had invited former oppositionists into government. In a striking break with the past, however, the new king allowed the creation of a Truth and Reconciliation Commission with public hearings that addressed violations of human rights – including disappearances, torture and murder – that occurred under his father. However the commission was not empowered to pursue suspected perpetrators on behalf of victims. Liberal critics of the process argued that the institution in whose interest abuses were committed, namely the monarchy itself, had not been held to account.

Moves in a democratic direction were carefully managed by the state, which retained its executive power through a classic system of patronage that acted as an informal or parallel bureaucracy under the monarch’s control. Political parties had little autonomy. Political pluralism or ‘
multi-partyism
’ – as encouraged by the electoral law introduced in 2002, tended to fractionalize opposition, enhancing the power of the king. As 
Amir

al-Mu
’minin
 or Commander of the Faithful – the king combines the supreme religious and political authority in his person, conferring upon him a 
legitimacy that Islamist opponents found hard to challenge. The radical Justice and Charity party, a vocal critic of the government, has been banned. The more pliant Islamist Justice and Development party had fared better, forming the third-largest bloc in the parliament.

In contrast to the ‘
asabiyya
 of the clans that ruled in Iraq and Syria and Libya, the Al Sa‘ud family in Saudi Arabia makes no attempt to conceal its ownership of the country’s principal natural resource. Since the state’s foundation in the 1920s the Al Sa‘ud, a clan of the ‘Aniza tribe, have effectively been its owners as well as its rulers. Oil is not just the kingdom’s primary national resource: it is first and foremost private family property. The bulk of the revenue is paid to the king before it is registered as national income. The royal family decides on its needs, and government officials are obliged to act accordingly. The 6,000-odd princes and princesses linked to the Al Sa‘ud are entitled to regular stipends in addition to their ‘working’ salaries as government officials or the 
commissions
 they may receive in business transactions. In 1996 a Saudi economist estimated that the royal family was costing the state at least $4 billion per year.

The structural weaknesses of the Saudi state – the only country in the world that takes its name from the ruling family – are compounded by the absence of a system of succession able to guarantee its continuity. Since the death of King ‘Abd al-‘Aziz in 1953 succession has passed down the line of his legitimate sons in general order of seniority. At this writing the present ruler, King ‘Abdullah, is 89. In 2011 and 2012 he was 
predeceased
 by two of his nominated heirs, Defence Minister Prince Sultan and the latter’s replacement, the much feared Interior Minister Prince Nayef. Though a decade younger than the king, Salman, the new Crown Prince, is known to have suffered at least one stroke. Although the Al Sa‘ud family has instituted an Allegiance Council to decide on matters of succession, the kingdom lacks formal mechanisms such as an elected parliament or independent supreme court to facilitate or legitimize change. The youngest surviving son of the founding monarch is thought to be nearing 70. In contrast to its gerontocratic rulers, the median ages of the Saudi population is well under 30. Given the way that separate business and political fiefdoms have developed among the vast number of the founder’s grandsons, the shift of power to the third generation is unlikely to be smooth.

THE CHALLENGE OF ISLAMISM

As the Arab world grew more distant from the period of direct colonial dominion, the older lines of ‘
asabiyya
 and dynastic rule reasserted 
themselves
. European influences brought new values and types of institution, but these lacked legitimacy, not least because they did not originate in indigenous traditions. The formal structures of statehood derived largely from the European experience (such as parliaments, political parties and Western-style civil society institutions) were soon subverted by more powerful social and political forces. The most formidable of the challenges facing governments in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries came from the Islamist movements. In the Sunni-majority traditions, these are divided into two broad tendencies represented by the Muslim Brothers, who accommodate modernist and reformist elements in their outlook and the more literalist or ‘fundamentalist’ Salafiyya movement, who look to the ‘pious ancestors’ (
al-salaf al-saleh
) or Prophet’s 
Companions
 for inspiration. As mentioned above, both were strongly 
represented
 in the 2011 Egyptian parliamentary elections, with the Salafists said to have been strongly supported with money from Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

28

 However, with the emergence of Iraq as a Shi‘i Arab state, populist and democratic values rooted in Shi‘i teachings and values have been influential in Bahrayn, Yemen and parts of Saudi Arabia where there are substantial Shi‘i communities.

The influence of religious discourse in the Arab-dominated regions of the Middle East and North Africa may be the consequence of an exponential leap in the level of urbanization that has decisively altered the cultural and demographic balance between urban and rural populations, creating a vast new proletariat of recently urbanized migrants susceptible to the messages of populist preachers and demagogues. Rapid 
urbanization
 – combined with modest improvements in healthcare – has led to declining living standards in many cities as government services failed to keep pace with demographic growth. During the Mubarak era, for example, the number of Egyptians living on the equivalent of less than $2 per day rose from 39 per cent to 43 per cent of the population, despite the increasingly flamboyant wealth exhibited by the country’s elites.

29

The Islamist movements through their welfare organizations were able to fill the gaps caused by government failures to deal with housing shortages and other social problems. Housing shortages in particular were forcing young people to delay marriage in societies where extra-marital 
sexual activity was strictly taboo. The resulting frustration, it could be argued, accounted for the strictness with which the Islamists sought to enforce rigid codes of sexual behaviour and dress. In non-oil states restrictions on welfare spending imposed by the International Monetary Fund led to withdrawal of the state from some areas and its replacement by Islamic welfare organizations and charitable associations. These voluntary organizations found generous sources of funding in Saudi 
Arabia
 and the Gulf. The Islamic financial sector, though tainted by scandal, provided employment opportunities and an avenue for building new 
networks
